content: 1. Begin with small amounts of physical activity and gradually increase the frequency, intensity, and duration over time to ensure a safe and effective progression. 2. Postpartum women should be informed by their healthcare provider about danger signs that indicate when to stop or limit physical activity. If these signs occur, they should consult a qualified health worker immediately. 3. Women should return to physical activity gradually after childbirth, particularly in cases of cesarean delivery, and this should be done in consultation with a healthcare provider. 4. Healthcare providers should offer advice tailored to the woman’s medical history and any contraindications to physical activity during the postpartum period. 5. Women who were habitually engaged in vigorous-intensity aerobic activity or were physically active before pregnancy can generally continue these activities during pregnancy and the postpartum period. 6. Sedentary behavior is defined as time spent sitting or lying down with low energy expenditure while awake, in contexts such as work, education, home, community settings, or transportation. 7. Comprehensive contraceptive information and services should be provided during postnatal care to ensure informed choices about modern contraception without discrimination. Privacy and confidentiality of medical and personal information must be respected. 8. The mode of birth does not restrict a postpartum woman’s contraceptive options. 9. Breastfeeding women who are six months postpartum or more can use progestogen-only pills (POPs), progestogen-only injectables (POIs), levonorgestrel (LNG), and etonogestrel (ETG) implants without restriction. Combined hormonal contraception (CHC) is generally acceptable. 10. A woman’s risk of HIV infection does not limit her contraceptive choices. Women are eligible to use all progestogen-only methods, copper intrauterine devices (Cu-IUDs), and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine devices (LNG-IUDs) without restriction. 11. Self-administered injectable contraception should be made available as an additional option for individuals of reproductive age, based on WHO guidelines and medical eligibility criteria. 12. WHO guidance includes other self-administered contraceptive methods such as the combined contraceptive patch, vaginal rings, and barrier methods like condoms, diaphragms, and cervical caps. Breastfeeding women can also use these methods alongside the lactational amenorrhea method during the first six months postpartum. 13. Ongoing competency-based training and supervision of health workers on delivering contraceptive education, information, and services should align with existing WHO guidelines. 14. Universal newborn screening for eye abnormalities is recommended and should be accompanied by diagnostic and management services for children identified with abnormalities. Screening should ideally occur before discharge from a health facility or at the first postnatal care visit after a home birth, within the first six weeks of life. 15. Newborn eye screening typically involves using a torchlight to examine external eye structures and red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope or suitable alternative. 16. Early detection of conditions that may adversely affect a newborn’s health and development is a critical component of quality postnatal care. Health workers should refer to WHO’s operational manual for detailed guidance on newborn assessment. 17. Neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, commonly presenting as jaundice, affects 60–80% of otherwise healthy newborns. While most cases are benign, severe jaundice can lead to acute bilirubin encephalopathy, kernicterus, or death if untreated. 18. Jaundice is clinically recognized through visual inspection, and serum bilirubin levels can be estimated non-invasively using a transcutaneous bilirubinometer or confirmed through blood sampling and laboratory analysis. 19. Universal newborn screening for congenital cataracts and other eye abnormalities is recommended. The red reflex test can detect a wide range of conditions, and screening should be performed by trained health workers. 20. Parents and families should be encouraged to seek healthcare early if they identify danger signs in their newborn, such as jaundice within the first 24 hours of life or yellow palms and soles at any age. 21. Women value clear and accurate information about their infant’s well-being, provided by knowledgeable and sensitive health workers. They also appreciate advice on neonatal development and want to feel confident and competent as mothers while adapting to their new roles and relationships. 22. Health workers should be adequately trained and equipped to provide postnatal care, including newborn examinations and counseling on screening procedures.
